title: Quadratic-form inequalities and singular values
subtitle: G2 lecture 061000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Standalone slide treatment of the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix; authored derivations, worked calculations and local SVG diagrams.

slides.title: From quadratic forms to ordered singular values
slides.lead: A pointwise inequality on vectors can control an entire singular-value list.
body: For self-adjoint operators H,K, the Loewner order H≼K means ⟨Hx,x⟩≤⟨Kx,x⟩ for every vector. When both are positive, the ordered eigenvalues are also ordered.
For rectangular maps A and B with the same source, compare their squared output lengths instead. That inequality is exactly the Loewner comparison of their source Gram operators.
slides.takeaway: Uniform output-length comparison is Gram-operator order.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · From quadratic forms to ordered singular values

slides.title: Positive operator order and min–max
slides.lead: Suppose 0≼H≼K are positive self-adjoint operators on the same finite-dimensional space.
body: For every nonzero vector, the Rayleigh quotient of H is no larger than the corresponding quotient of K. The Courant–Fischer formula computes each ordered eigenvalue by taking the same max-over-subspaces of a minimum Rayleigh quotient.
Because the pointwise inequality survives both optimization steps, λⱼ(H)≤λⱼ(K) for every j.
slides.takeaway: Courant–Fischer transports form order to every eigenvalue.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Positive operator order and min–max

slides.title: Why positivity is essential
slides.lead: A positive operator has singular values equal to its nonnegative eigenvalues.
body: Consequently the preceding eigenvalue monotonicity immediately gives σⱼ(H)≤σⱼ(K) when 0≼H≼K. For arbitrary self-adjoint matrices with negative eigenvalues, ordering the eigenvalues does not order their absolute values.
This is why the same statement cannot be applied blindly to singular values of indefinite self-adjoint matrices.
slides.takeaway: Nonnegative spectrum connects eigenvalue order to singular-value order.

slides.title: Apply the theorem to rectangular maps
slides.lead: Maps A:E→F and B:E→G may have different codomains; their Gram operators still act on the same source E.
body: If every input satisfies ||Ax||²≤||Bx||², then A*A≼B*B. Courant–Fischer orders the eigenvalues of these positive Gram matrices, and taking square roots orders their singular values.
No common output space or choice of output frames is needed to state the result.
slides.takeaway: Gram order compares singular values even when target dimensions differ.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Apply the theorem to rectangular maps

slides.title: A rectangular numerical calculation
slides.lead: Let A:ℝ²→ℝ³ have orthogonal output columns of lengths three and one.
body: Let B:ℝ²→ℝ⁴ have orthogonal output columns of lengths four and two. Then A*A=diag(9,1) and B*B=diag(16,4), so the difference is diag(7,3), which is positive.
The singular-value lists are (3,1) and (4,2), and the theorem gives both inequalities simultaneously.
slides.takeaway: The comparison works through a shared source even for different codomains.

slides.title: Squaring a Loewner inequality can fail
slides.lead: For positive semidefinite matrices, H≼K does not generally imply H²≼K².
body: Take H=diag(1,0) and K=[[2,1],[1,1]]. The difference K−H=[[1,1],[1,1]] is positive, so H≼K. But K²−H²=[[4,3],[3,2]] has determinant 8−9=−1 and therefore is indefinite.
The failure comes from noncommutativity: scalar squaring does not preserve Loewner order for arbitrary positive matrices.
slides.takeaway: Do not square positive operator inequalities without an appropriate additional theorem.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Squaring a Loewner inequality can fail

slides.title: Why the square-root method is legitimate
slides.lead: The rectangular singular-value comparison does not require squaring an arbitrary operator inequality.
body: Instead, it starts with A*A≼B*B, applies eigenvalue min–max to those already-positive Gram operators, and then takes scalar square roots of the ordered nonnegative eigenvalues.
The scalar function t↦√t is increasing on nonnegative numbers. That elementary final step is safe and suffices for singular-value monotonicity.
slides.takeaway: Scalar monotonicity after min–max is different from squaring matrices in Loewner order.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Why the square-root method is legitimate

slides.title: A trace inequality is weaker information
slides.lead: If 0≼H≼K, the trace of K−H is nonnegative, so tr H≤tr K.
body: This yields only one aggregate scalar comparison. Eigenvalue monotonicity is stronger: it controls every ordered eigenvalue separately and therefore all singular-value prefixes as well.
A proof that establishes only the trace inequality cannot automatically be cited as an entrywise eigenvalue theorem; Courant–Fischer provides the missing information.
slides.takeaway: Trace comparison summarizes size, while min–max preserves each ordered spectral value.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · A trace inequality is weaker information

slides.title: Where gap estimates enter later
slides.lead: Quadratic-form inequalities and singular values are tools for solving operator equations under spectral separation.
body: A Sylvester equation has the form AX−XB=C. A separation condition on the spectral sets of A and B creates a gap that allows us to bound X by C.
The same proof toolkit—positive operators, form order, and singular-value comparison—will transfer operator inequalities into norm bounds on spectral-subspace motion.
slides.takeaway: Form order is one route from spectral separation to quantitative operator estimates.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Where gap estimates enter later

slides.title: Reconstruct both the theorem and the warning
slides.lead: Start from an inequality ||Ax||²≤||Bx||² holding for every common input.
body: Translate it into source Gram order, apply Courant–Fischer, and take scalar square roots to obtain singular-value domination. Check the steps using the rectangular example with Gram matrices diag(9,1) and diag(16,4).
Then multiply out H=diag(1,0) and K=[[2,1],[1,1]] to see why the apparently similar operation of squaring a Loewner inequality fails.
slides.takeaway: A valid min–max comparison and an invalid operator squaring step must remain distinct.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 061000 · Reconstruct both the theorem and the warning
